title: AWS Well-Architected Agent: least-privilege setup and how to check its advice
summary: Set up the new AWS Well-Architected Agent with roles you control, review Terraform before deploying, and vet each AI recommendation against your own metrics and plans.

html:
The short version The AWS Well-Architected Agent reads your accounts through roles you create and suggests fixes for cost, security, resilience and performance. Run it from a dedicated account, decide how much it may read before you attach the managed policy, and treat every recommendation as a proposal: check it against your own metrics and a terraform plan before anything reaches production.

AWS put the Well-Architected Agent into public preview on 1 October 2026. Instead of a yearly questionnaire, it scans your accounts every week, ranks findings against goals you write in plain language, and hands back fixes as console steps, CLI commands or updated infrastructure as code (IaC). It also reviews Terraform or CDK projects before you deploy them.

That is useful, and it is also an AI service asking for broad read access to production. The preview is only days old, so there are no independent accuracy reports yet. This guide covers the setup decisions that matter and a simple routine for checking what it tells you. Everything here comes from AWS's documentation; preview details can change.

1Check that it fits before you start

Four facts decide whether the agent is for you right now:

  • Support plan. The user guide requires Business+ or higher: Business+, Enterprise On-Ramp, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations. Developer and Business plans have no access, even though the launch post only says "an AWS Support plan".

  • Regions. Profiles are hosted in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio) or US West (Oregon). From there the agent can scan resources in every commercial Region, so configuration data from, say, an EU workload is read by a service running in the US.

  • Pillars. It covers four areas: cost optimization, security, resilience and performance. Operational excellence and sustainability, the framework's other two pillars, are not on the list.

  • Price. AWS has not published a price for the preview. Do not assume it is free.

Also note the preview terms. AWS's service terms say service level agreements do not apply to previews, and that previews should not be used to process sensitive data unless AWS says otherwise. If you run regulated workloads, such as healthcare systems under HIPAA, settle that question with your compliance owner before you connect production accounts.

2Set up the two-role chain from a dedicated account

The agent does not use a service-linked role. You create two kinds of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role yourself, which keeps you in control of what it can reach:

  • Execution role, in the account that owns the agent profile. The wellarchitected.amazonaws.com service assumes it, and its only permission is sts:AssumeRole on the access roles.

  • Access role, one in every workload account you want scanned. It trusts the execution role and carries the read-only scanning policy.

AWS recommends running profiles from a dedicated account with no production workloads, trusting the execution role's ARN rather than the whole account, and watching CloudTrail for the agent's activity. The console can create the execution role for you, but it never creates the access roles. You add one to each workload account, all with the same name:

JSON{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/service-role/ExecutionRoleForWellArchitectedAgent"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

If you manage accounts with Terraform, the same role is a few resources you can roll out everywhere. The last two blocks are optional and explained in the next step:

Terraform# Deploy in every workload account the agent should scan.
variable "profile_account_id" {
  type        = string
  description = "Account that owns the Well-Architected Agent profile"
}

variable "execution_role_name" {
  type    = string
  default = "ExecutionRoleForWellArchitectedAgent"
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "trust_wa_agent" {
  statement {
    actions = ["sts:AssumeRole"]
    principals {
      type = "AWS"
      # Console-created execution roles live under service-role/.
      identifiers = ["arn:aws:iam::${var.profile_account_id}:role/service-role/${var.execution_role_name}"]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_role" "wa_agent_access" {
  name               = "AccessRoleForWellArchitectedAgent"
  assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.trust_wa_agent.json
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "wa_agent_scanning" {
  role       = aws_iam_role.wa_agent_access.name
  policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/WellArchitectedAgentResourceScanning"
}

# Optional: keep log, source and query contents out of reach.
data "aws_iam_policy_document" "wa_agent_no_content" {
  statement {
    effect = "Deny"
    actions = [
      "logs:GetLogEvents",
      "logs:FilterLogEvents",
      "codecommit:GetBlob",
      "codecommit:GetFile",
      "athena:GetQueryResults",
    ]
    resources = ["*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "wa_agent_no_content" {
  name   = "DenyContentReads"
  role   = aws_iam_role.wa_agent_access.id
  policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.wa_agent_no_content.json
}
Common mistakeA console-created execution role lives under the service-role/ path, so its ARN is arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/service-role/ExecutionRoleForWellArchitectedAgent. If you created the role yourself, the path is absent. A mismatch here is the most common reason the agent cannot reach an account.

3Decide what "read-only" should mean for you

The recommended access policy, WellArchitectedAgentResourceScanning, contains only Get, Describe, List and BatchGet actions, so the agent cannot change anything. Read-only is not the same as metadata-only, though. The policy includes logs:Get*, which covers reading log events, codecommit:Get*, which covers source files, athena:Get*, which covers query results, and lambda:GetFunction, which returns a function's environment variables and a link to download its code. It does not include s3:GetObject or secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.

AWS allows a narrower custom policy. A middle ground is the explicit deny in the Terraform above: it blocks log, source-code and query-result contents while keeping the configuration reads the agent relies on. Expect fewer findings for those services. Any permission the agent is refused shows up in its generation records, so you can see what it skipped.

Whatever you choose, this is a good moment to move secrets out of Lambda environment variables and logs. Anything stored there is readable by every principal with this policy, not only the agent.

4Create the profile, a goal and an application context

A profile names the accounts, Regions and pillars to analyse, up to 100 accounts. It also needs at least one goal and at least one application context. Without an application context the profile is marked invalid and nothing is generated. You can do this in the console, or with the AWS CLI. The API never creates IAM roles, so complete step 2 first:

Bashaws wellarchitected create-agent-profile \
  --name platform-review \
  --execution-role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/service-role/ExecutionRoleForWellArchitectedAgent \
  --pillars COST_OPTIMIZATION SECURITY RESILIENCE PERFORMANCE \
  --deletion-protection \
  --aggregation-configuration '[{"accountId":"444455556666","accessRoleArn":"arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/AccessRoleForWellArchitectedAgent","regions":["us-east-1","eu-west-1"]}]'

PROFILE=arn:aws:wellarchitected:us-east-1:111122223333:agent-profile/platform-review

aws wellarchitected create-agent-goal --profile-arn "$PROFILE" \
  --title "Cut monthly EC2 and RDS spend by 15% without lowering availability" \
  --pillars COST_OPTIMIZATION RESILIENCE

aws wellarchitected create-agent-context --profile-arn "$PROFILE" \
  --title "Patient portal API" --context-type APPLICATION \
  --content '{"applicationOverview":"Multi-tenant REST API on PostgreSQL","criticality":"BUSINESS_CRITICAL","accountIds":["444455556666"],"regions":["eu-west-1"]}'

aws wellarchitected get-agent-profile --profile-arn "$PROFILE" \
  --query '{eligible: eligibleForScheduledGeneration, errors: fieldErrors}'

Goals are what the agent ranks against, so make them measurable and honest about trade-offs. When the profile is eligible, the first scheduled recommendations arrive within 48 hours. After that they refresh weekly, at most 30 per run, and you cannot trigger resource or application recommendations on demand.

Cost figures deserve one decision up front. Without AWS Cost Explorer, the agent estimates savings from public list prices, which ignore your Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and discounts. Turning on Cost Explorer with resource-level daily data gives real numbers. It is enabled per account, cannot be turned off once enabled, and its granular data and API requests are charged.

5Review IaC before it is deployed

Architecture reviews are the part most teams can use straight away, because they run before anything reaches an account. You zip your project, upload it to an S3 bucket in the same Region as the profile, and start a review. Results come back as recommendations with updated code in the same language, so Terraform in means Terraform out.

Bashcd infra && zip -r ../pr-142.zip . -x '.terraform/*' '*.tfstate*'
aws s3 cp ../pr-142.zip s3://my-iac-reviews/pr-142.zip --region us-east-1

aws wellarchitected start-agent-recommendation-generation \
  --profile-arn "$PROFILE" \
  --types ARCHITECTURE \
  --name terraform-pr-142 \
  --scope '{"pillars":["SECURITY","RESILIENCE"]}' \
  --additional-context '{"s3Uri":"s3://my-iac-reviews/pr-142.zip","lensArns":["arn:aws:wellarchitected::aws:lens/wellarchitected"]}'

aws wellarchitected list-agent-recommendation-generations --profile-arn "$PROFILE"

Limits to plan around:

  • A .zip can be at most 25 MB; an S3 folder at most 100 MB, with no file over 1 MB.

  • Five reviews per day per profile.

  • Only the core Well-Architected Framework lens is available, not the Serverless, SaaS or generative AI lenses.

  • The review page lists CDK and Terraform as supported. Other AWS pages also mention CloudFormation, so test a plain CloudFormation template before relying on it.

Keep state files, .terraform folders and any secrets out of the archive, as the zip exclusions above do. The console also asks you to consent to the agent reading the file.

6Check every recommendation before acting

AWS is clear that AI-generated recommendations may be wrong or incomplete, and that you are responsible for evaluating them. Application-level recommendations are still labelled beta. The agent never runs AI-generated steps for you. Only fixes that come from Trusted Advisor checks have pre-built Systems Manager runbooks it can run with your consent.

Three checks catch most bad advice:

  1. Freshness. Each recommendation's timestamp updates every weekly cycle. One without a recent update may describe a resource that has already changed.

  2. Peaks, not averages. For rightsizing, compare against AWS Compute Optimizer. It looks back 14 days by default; switch to 32 days, which costs nothing extra and catches monthly batch jobs, and look at 99th-percentile (P99) utilisation. An instance that averages 8% CPU but hits 85% at month end should not shrink.

  3. The diff. Put suggested IaC changes through your normal pipeline and read the plan. Replacements (-/+) and any widened IAM permissions deserve a second reviewer.

Bashterraform plan -out=agent-fix.tfplan -detailed-exitcode   # exit code 2 = there are changes
terraform show agent-fix.tfplan | grep -E '^\s*-/\+|must be replaced'   # replacements need a second look
terraform apply agent-fix.tfplan                                          # applies exactly what you reviewed
# Plan files contain sensitive values in plain text: never commit them.

For CDK, cdk diff --security-only shows only changes that broaden security, and --fail turns any difference into a failing continuous integration (CI) step. This caution is not specific to AWS: in the IaC-Eval benchmark, published at NeurIPS 2024, GPT-4 produced correct Terraform for AWS on the first try in only 19.36% of tasks. Generated infrastructure code needs the same review as code from a new teammate.

Close the loop in the agent too. Mark recommendations you will not act on as suppressed with a reason, for example with update-agent-recommendation-status --status SUPPRESSED --update-reason "...", so the list stays useful.

Common mistakesCreating the profile but no application context, then waiting for results that never come. Trusting dollar figures without Cost Explorer. Reading a short list as a clean bill of health: the agent skips many resource types, including AWS::WAFv2::WebACL and AWS::OpenSearchService::Domain, so silence about them means nothing. Applying generated IaC without reading the plan.

What it does not replace

The agent builds on services you may already use. It draws on findings and signals from Trusted Advisor, Compute Optimizer, Security Hub CSPM, Resilience Hub and Cost Optimization Hub, and adds goal-based ranking and ready-made fixes. Blind spots in those sources carry through.

It also cannot see how your team works. The framework describes a review as "a conversation and not an audit": the people who built and run the system, talking through trade-offs and one-way decisions. Operational excellence and sustainability are not covered by the agent at all. Use it to keep the obvious issues from piling up between reviews, and keep the conversation for the decisions that need people.
